Q2  THE ORACLE'S OWN BLINDNESS: does the SINK repl row distinguish the
    ORIGINAL node from a REBUILT one?
==============================================================================
  uop_short(replacement)   = 'SINK'        <- what gr-oracle.py prints
  replacement is original  = False
  replacement op.name      = SINK
  replacement.src == orig.src = False
  replacement.src is orig.src = False
  replacement.key == orig.key = False

  `uop_short` prints only `u.op.name` for a SINK, so it answers 'SINK'
  for the original node AND for a rebuilt node AND for any node whose
  srcs were rewritten. The repl row is therefore blind, ON THE CPYTHON
  SIDE, to the identity invariant walk_rewrite actually turns on.
  The two-lane gate can agree on this row for the wrong reason.

==============================================================================
Q3  WHAT `pm_post_sched_cache` ACTUALLY CONTAINS (read off the patterns)
==============================================================================
  UPat(op=PARAM) fields=None -> src-visible=False
  UPat(op=ALLOC) fields=None -> src-visible=False
  rule count: 2

  A rule that READS a node's srcs is what makes `u` and `rebuilt`
  different arguments: `src(rebuilt,0)` is the REWRITTEN src and
  `src(u,0)` is the original. pm_post_sched_cache carries no such rule,
  so a fixture built only from PARAM/ALLOC/SINK cannot separate them and
  NO NUMBER OF SUCH FIXTURES EVER WILL. That is a closed case.
